sections.normalized_html:
Consider a system of two linear equations in two variables, represented by the matrix equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}] in the usual way. Given that the system has exactly one solution, which of the following statements are true?

  1. [MATH: \det(A) =0]

  2. The system [MATH: [2; 2]] has exactly one solution

  3. [MATH: A^{-1}] does not exist
sections.readable_text:
Consider a system of two linear equations in two variables, represented by the matrix equation [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}] in the usual way. Given that the system has exactly one solution, which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: \det(A) =0]
2. The system [MATH: [2; 2]] has exactly one solution
3. [MATH: A^{-1}] does not exist

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that given [MATH: [a_{11}|a_{12}; a_{21}|a_{22}]], then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:

  1. [MATH: A] is invertible.

  2. The system [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}] has exactly one solution for any [MATH: 2 \times 1] column vector [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

  3. The system [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}] has the unique zero solution.

  4. The lines [MATH: a_{11}x+a_{12}y=b_1] and [MATH: a_{21}x+a_{22}y=b_2] intersect at exactly one point.

  5. [MATH: \det(A) \neq 0.]

Also, we are told that the second part of the invertible matrix theorem is true. So, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

  • Statement I is false by the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem.

  • Statement II is true by the second part of the invertible matrix theorem.

  • Statement III is false by the first part of the invertible matrix theorem.

Therefore, only statement II is true.
